changes.before: Encorafenib blocks the BRAF V600 growth signal in eligible melanoma cells. Binimetinib acts further down the same pathway. They have different dose schedules and different safety decisions, so the prescription for one must not be assumed to apply to the other.
changes.after: Encorafenib blocks altered BRAF signalling in eligible melanoma. Binimetinib acts at a different step in the same growth pathway. Each medicine retains its own dosing and safety instructions.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-ema-braftovi

changes.before: Binimetinib inhibits MEK in the cell-growth pathway. It can also affect normal muscle, heart and retinal tissues. CK blood tests, heart checks and prompt reporting of eye or muscle changes help the team identify problems before they become more serious.
changes.after: Binimetinib inhibits MEK proteins in the growth-signalling pathway. Alongside effects on cancer cells, it can affect muscle, heart and retinal tissue. The prescribed blood and heart checks and prompt review of new eye symptoms help detect these effects.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-ema-mektovi

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-melanoma

changes.before: Keep the pathology summary, original skin site, stage and details of any lymph-node involvement together. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the original melanoma; they are different from the stage. If the diagnosis arose in the eye or a mucosal surface, ask whether this cutaneous-melanoma information applies.
changes.after: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-melanoma-clinical

changes.before: A BRAF V600 result helps decide whether the BRAF/MEK targeted medicines in this guide are suitable. This is usually a test of the tumour, not proof of an inherited family condition. Keep the actual result and test date; ask about genetic counselling only when your personal or family history makes that relevant.
changes.after: A BRAF V600 result identifies whether the targeted medicines in this plan can act on the tumour. Keep the laboratory result and date. A tumour change is not, on its own, evidence of an inherited condition.

changes.before: Record what surgery removed and whether the present medicine is postoperative treatment to lower recurrence risk or treatment of cancer that remains or has spread. Radiotherapy, stereotactic treatment or another operation may have a separate role; their timing and side effects need their own plan.
changes.after: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-melanoma

changes.before: Stage describes the extent of melanoma at diagnosis or a later reassessment. A response assessment asks how known cancer has changed with treatment. In the adjuvant setting there may be no visible tumour to measure: surveillance looks for recurrence while safety checks look for medicine effects.
changes.after: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-melanoma

changes.before: Continue to report a new or changing mole, a non-healing lesion, a new lump or an unexplained persistent symptom. Do not assume every new lesion is melanoma, and do not use a photograph or a good response at one site to rule out a problem elsewhere.
changes.after: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

changes.before: Record surgery, radiotherapy and other anticancer medicines separately, including dates and the specialist responsible. This schedule does not automatically include or authorise another treatment. Ask whether any overlap changes tests, symptoms to report or the timing of appointments.
changes.after: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

changes.before: Arrange medicine supply, transport, interpreter or carer support before it is needed. Bring the alert card, symptom record and questions. Ask which appointments require someone to accompany you and how to obtain urgent advice outside normal hours.
changes.after: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

changes.before: For each test, record its purpose, due date, result and action. Agree how results reach you and who checks a result from another hospital. If an appointment or result has not arrived, contact the named service rather than assuming no news means no action is needed.
changes.after: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-nutrition

changes.before: Tell the team early about nausea, taste change, a sore mouth, diarrhoea or falling weight. Ask for an individual fluid and food plan if heart, kidney or other conditions limit intake. Gentle activity and planned rest can help maintain function; adjust to symptoms and ask for support when fatigue limits daily life.
changes.after: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-sunsmart

changes.before: Use shade, protective clothing, a hat and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, and avoid tanning beds. Reapply sunscreen according to its instructions. Protection matters even when it is cloudy; choose a practical approach that lets you remain active safely.
changes.after: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-skin

changes.before: Ask how to examine your skin, scars and relevant lymph-node areas and how often your own team recommends doing so. A mirror or a trusted helper can make hard-to-see areas easier to check. Report a new or changing lesion, a non-healing sore or a new lump rather than waiting for a routine visit.
changes.after: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

changes.before: If useful, keep a dated photograph with consistent lighting and a size reference, following your team’s advice. Photographs are optional and do not diagnose a cancer or replace examination. Keep them privately; this printable passport does not require you to upload images or other personal health information.
changes.after: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-skin

changes.before: Use the dressings and skin-care plan recommended for your lesion and treatment. Ask before applying new creams or remedies to an open or treated area. Worsening pain, discharge, redness, bleeding or loss of function needs advice; routine skin-care instructions are not a substitute for assessment.
changes.after: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

changes.before: Ask what evidence applies to your diagnosis, stage, biomarker and treatment setting, what outcome the team hopes to improve, and what may happen without this treatment. A trial average cannot predict an individual result; a benefit measured in one setting should not be transferred to another.
changes.after: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-palliative

changes.before: Discuss other suitable treatments, clinical trials if relevant, local treatment options and symptom-focused care. Ask when the decision will be reviewed and what would prompt a change. Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life alongside anticancer treatment.
changes.after: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

changes.before: Tell the team about work, transport, caring responsibilities, cost concerns, body image, anxiety or sleep. Ask which nurse, social worker, dietitian, rehabilitation professional or support organisation can help. Use resources relevant to your country and service; a US guide may describe different access or funding.
changes.after: Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.

changes.before: Ask someone on the team to check that you can explain the medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route in your own words. An interpreter, large-print copy or a trusted supporter can help; none requires you to use a smartphone.
changes.after: Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.

changes.before: Follow-up depends on stage, treatment and symptoms. Your team records the skin/lymph-node examination plan, whether body or brain imaging is needed, and which service owns each appointment. A general patient booklet does not set a universal scan interval for every patient.
changes.after: Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.

changes.before: This handbook can be used without a phone: keep the schedule, symptom advice, medicine list, tests and contacts together. The QR code is an optional route to the matching regimen information. Ask the team to print updates when your plan changes and keep the latest dated copy.
changes.after: Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.

changes.before: The evidence discussion must match the diagnosis, biomarker and treatment setting shown in this guide.
changes.after: Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.

before: Individual benefit and risk cannot be predicted from a group average.
The supplied NCCN patient guide is an education reference, not Irish prescribing or reimbursement authority.
This handoff does not claim a completed independent quantitative trial-benefit audit.
after: Individual benefit and risk cannot be predicted from a group average.
Your team explains the evidence that applies to this treatment plan and the uncertainty for you as an individual.

changes.before: Arrange dates, medicine supply, transport and any needed interpreter or carer support. Ask whether bloods are taken in the oncology unit or elsewhere and how the result reaches the prescriber.
changes.after: Plan blood tests, travel and medicine collection in advance. If you need an interpreter or someone to help at home, tell the team before the appointment.

changes.before: Keep this complete handbook, the three-page summary and the wallet card together. The QR code is optional. Ask the team to add your actual contacts and print a revised plan when treatment changes.
changes.after: Ask for your latest schedule and contact details on paper. Replace old versions when treatment changes so everyone helping you uses the same plan.

changes.before: Follow-up depends on stage, treatment and symptoms. Your team records the skin/lymph-node examination plan, whether body or brain imaging is needed, and which service owns each appointment. A general patient booklet does not set a universal scan interval for every patient.
changes.after: Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.

before.title: Your PRRT course
before.intro: Receptor-directed radiation with specialist safety checks.

items.title: Why PRRT?
items.text: PRRT carries radiation to somatostatin receptors on NET cells to help control disease that cannot be removed or has spread. A specialist NET and nuclear-medicine team checks receptor imaging, organ function and your priorities before recommending it.

items.title: How it works
items.text: Lutathera joins a receptor-binding molecule to the radioactive element lutetium-177. After infusion, it attaches to somatostatin receptors on suitable NET cells and delivers radiation nearby. The receptor scan helps select patients. Kidneys and blood-forming marrow can also receive radiation, which is why kidney protection and long-term blood monitoring matter.

items.title: Why the amino acids matter
items.text: The amino-acid infusion reduces the amount of radioactive medicine retained in the kidneys. It is an essential part of kidney protection. It can cause nausea and affect potassium or fluid balance, so anti-sickness treatment, blood tests and observation are needed.

items.title: Four intended administrations
items.text: Four administrations are planned, usually eight weeks apart. Lutathera is infused over about 30–40 minutes, with a four-hour kidney-protective amino-acid infusion and anti-sickness treatment. The visit is much longer than the Lutathera infusion; an overnight stay may be needed.

items.title: Evidence and its limits
items.text: Lutetium-177 DOTATATE with standard-dose octreotide improved time before progression compared with high-dose octreotide. The final overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. The findings do not promise a survival gain for an individual. NETTER-1 was a midgut study. Its results must not be presented as identical evidence for every pancreatic, other GI or grade 3 NET. The current Irish eligibility and specialist decision determine this regimen’s use.

before.title: Preparing for hospital and returning home
before.intro: The service supplies a personal written plan.

items.title: Before admission
items.text: Confirm SSTR imaging, appointments, recent bloods, hormone medicines and pregnancy precautions. Tell the team about kidney/heart problems, incontinence, a catheter, childcare or close contact with pregnant people; these may change the practical plan.

items.title: Treatment day
items.text: The standard NCCP activity is 7.4 GBq by intravenous infusion, usually every eight weeks for four administrations; the specialist may alter, delay or stop treatment. Lutathera runs over approximately 30–40 minutes. A lysine/arginine amino-acid infusion starts 30 minutes beforehand and continues for four hours. An anti-sickness medicine is given at least 30 minutes before the amino acids. The first visit generally includes an overnight stay; later treatments may be day case or overnight. The service confirms your plan.

items.title: SSA injections: stop and restart
items.text: The NET and nuclear-medicine teams must coordinate the injection plan. Do not translate “about four weeks” into your own date: NCCP specifies 30 days for long-acting SSA and 24 hours for short-acting SSA before PRRT. Restart timing follows the written service plan; it can differ with day-case arrangements.

items.title: At home after treatment
items.text: Follow individual instructions on distance and time with other people, sleeping arrangements, toilets, body fluids, laundry, work and transport. Restrictions may extend to three weeks for some contacts. Contact the medical physicist before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.

items.title: Travel and other healthcare
items.text: Carry the discharge letter and treatment card, including the date and type of radioactive treatment. Ask about travel and radiation detectors. Tell any healthcare staff you have had PRRT; urgent care must never be delayed because of radiation precautions.

before.title: Blood tests, scans and follow-up
before.intro: Tests continue between treatments and after the course.

items.title: The full safety-test sequence
items.text: Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, ECHO/MUGA and pregnancy assessment where applicable. Counts/kidneys/liver once 2–4 weeks before and shortly before each infusion, every two weeks between, then every four weeks for at least three months after the final dose and every three months for the following year. Potassium is checked before amino acids. Renal monitoring continues at least through the first year. Post-infusion radiation scans and response scans have separate purposes.

items.title: What may change treatment
items.text: The specialist may postpone, reduce or stop treatment for low counts, kidney/liver abnormalities, other toxicity or disease change. A four-stamp record shows intended administrations; it cannot confirm medical suitability.

items.title: Post-treatment scans
items.text: The Irish service describes special scans after each infusion to measure radiation delivered to organs. CT/MRI or other scans to assess tumour response follow the specialist plan.

items.title: Delayed effects
items.text: Kidney injury and rare bone-marrow disorders, including myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukaemia, can occur later. Persistent tiredness, infections, bruising or bleeding needs review even after the treatment course.

before.title: Urgent symptoms, hormone safety and precautions

items.title: When to seek help
items.text: Seek urgent help for sudden severe flushing with faintness, severe diarrhoea, wheeze or breathing trouble, especially in the first 48 hours; follow the hormone-crisis plan. Fever, bleeding, much less urine, persistent severe abdominal pain, muscle weakness or confusion needs prompt advice. Tell emergency staff when you received PRRT; radiation precautions must not delay urgent care.

items.title: Hormone crisis
items.text: PRRT can trigger a sudden hormone release. The Irish leaflet highlights the first 48 hours as the main early-risk period. Staff monitor you and may give extra medicines or extend the stay. You need clear instructions for symptoms after discharge; a history of hormone symptoms affects planning.

items.title: Tumour breakdown and fluid changes
items.text: Rapid tumour breakdown can disturb blood chemistry. New muscle cramps, weakness, confusion, palpitations, reduced urine or breathlessness needs prompt assessment. Staff also monitor potassium and fluid balance around the amino-acid infusion.

items.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
items.text: Lutathera can harm an unborn child and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for seven months after the last dose for patients who could become pregnant; men with partners who could become pregnant need contraception during treatment and for four months afterwards. Breastfeeding must stop before treatment; follow specialist advice.

items.title: If a visit is delayed
items.text: The team decides whether a delayed administration remains suitable and whether activity must change. Do not assume a treatment can automatically proceed at the maximum interval. Continue the blood-test and symptom plan.

items.title: Contacts and paperwork
items.text: Write the actual NET, PRRT nursing and radiation-protection contacts on the paper plan. Example numbers are not clinical contact lines. Keep the written precautions and urgent hormone-symptom instructions with the discharge letter.

before.title: Your Irish PRRT service plan in print
before.intro: Confirm bookings and restrictions with the treating service.

items.title: The Irish service’s scan appointments
items.text: The detailed Irish leaflet describes three radiation-assessment scans on separate days in the first week after the first infusion, starting the next day, and one scan after later infusions. It also describes CT or MRI between the second and third infusions and after the course. These are service arrangements to confirm on your appointment sheet, not a universal timetable for every NET.

items.title: Extra blood tests after the course
items.text: NCCP specifies four-weekly blood tests for at least three months, then three-monthly for the following year. The Irish service leaflet also describes fortnightly tests for eight weeks immediately after the final infusion. Your written discharge plan may therefore require more frequent early tests; follow that plan and ask the service to resolve any mismatch.

items.title: Paper radiation instructions for home
items.text: Before discharge, obtain a paper copy with the exact end date for each restriction. The Irish leaflet includes daily bathing, careful handwashing, sitting to pass urine and separate washing of body-fluid-soiled laundry in the first week. Ask for specific handling instructions for pads, incontinence or a catheter. Sleeping, travel, work and contact limits differ: examples include separate beds from a partner for 14 days and sleeping apart from pregnant people or children for three weeks. Your medical physicist’s personal instructions take precedence.

items.title: Carry the official radiation card too
items.text: The medical physicist supplies a radiation-treatment card to carry for the time stated. The SACTCheck wallet card is an additional treatment record and does not replace that official card, the discharge letter or the radiation-safety plan.

before.title: Understanding your particular NET
before.intro: Several different features help the team choose treatment.

items.title: Where it started and where it is now
items.text: A neuroendocrine tumour (NET) starts in cells that receive signals and can release hormones. The original organ is the primary site. A pancreatic NET is different from the more common pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Stage describes how far the cancer has spread; the stage system depends on its original site. A tumour in the liver may be a NET that spread there from elsewhere.

items.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
items.text: Differentiation describes how the cells look under the microscope. Grade describes their growth activity. Ki-67 is a laboratory measure of the proportion of tumour cells showing a marker of cell growth and helps assess grade in relevant NETs. It is not the percentage of your body affected and is not a survival percentage. Ask for the exact pathology wording, grade and Ki-67 result, including the sample date.

items.title: Grade is different from stage
items.text: A low-grade NET can have spread, and a high-grade tumour is not automatically stage 4. Well-differentiated grade 3 NET and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are different diagnoses with different treatment choices. These medicine guides must not be applied to another diagnosis simply because its name contains neuroendocrine.

items.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
items.text: A functioning NET causes a hormone-related syndrome. A nonfunctioning NET does not cause a recognisable excess-hormone syndrome, but it can still grow or cause symptoms by its size or location. Ask which description applies to you. A positive somatostatin receptor scan does not by itself mean the tumour is functioning.

items.title: Your diagnosis record
items.text: Keep the primary site, differentiation, grade, Ki-67 if reported, stage or sites of spread, hormone syndrome and receptor-scan result together in your passport. Ask the team to explain changes rather than trying to interpret one result in isolation.

before.title: Making sense of tests and results
before.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and hormone tests answer different questions.

items.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
items.text: Blood counts measure infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests help the team assess how your body can handle treatment. The schedule for your medicine is shown separately. Attend these checks even when you feel well; a scan does not replace them.

items.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
items.text: CT and MRI help show tumour size and where it is. A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) scan looks for receptor targets that certain treatments can attach to. An FDG-PET scan answers a different question about tumour activity and may be useful in selected cases. You will not necessarily need every scan. The specialist decides which test can change your care.

items.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
items.text: The team may measure selected blood or urine markers when they answer a question about your NET or symptoms. These can include serotonin-related testing such as 5-HIAA for selected patients, or specific pancreatic hormones. Chromogranin A is not a universal test before every treatment. A changing marker alone does not prove cancer growth. Record why each test is being done, how to prepare and who will explain it.

items.title: Preparing for a test
items.text: Ask whether you need fasting, a timed urine collection, dietary preparation or a medicine review. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for your particular test. Do not stop an acid-suppressing medicine, diabetes medicine or hormone-control treatment yourself. Tell the team about kidney problems, allergies and all medicines before a scan or blood test.

items.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
items.text: A heart ultrasound may be needed for particular treatment risks or to assess heart-valve problems associated with a hormone syndrome. It is not required on the same timetable for every NET. Depending on the diagnosis, age and family history, the team may offer genetic counselling; some NETs occur with inherited conditions such as MEN1. A tumour gene test and an inherited-risk test are not interchangeable.

items.title: Who does what, and when?
items.text: Use the passport to write each test, its purpose, planned date, booking service, result-review contact and next step. Your consultant sets response-scan and marker intervals. The postoperative schedules in general guides are not automatically the right schedule while you are taking these medicines.

before.title: Hormone symptoms and day-to-day changes
before.intro: A new symptom may come from the NET, treatment or another illness.

items.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
items.text: Record your usual bowel pattern, flushing, pain, appetite, weight and energy before starting. Note what changes, how long it lasts, what you were taking and how it affects daily life. This helps the team distinguish a hormone problem from treatment toxicity without assuming that every symptom is cancer progression.

items.title: Hormone-related symptoms
items.text: Depending on the tumour, excess hormones may cause flushing, frequent watery stools, wheezing, acid-related pain or blood-sugar disturbances. An insulin-producing tumour can cause low blood sugar. Not every NET causes these problems. Ask which symptoms matter for your diagnosis and whether you need a separate rescue plan.

items.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
items.text: Somatostatin analogue injections and other symptom treatments may continue alongside anticancer treatment when prescribed. They may have their own appointment dates. Never stop them simply because tablets are paused. PRRT requires a carefully coordinated interruption and restart plan, which the nuclear-medicine service must supply.

items.title: When a change is urgent
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency plan for sudden or severe symptoms. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency assessment. Severe diarrhoea, persistent vomiting, dehydration, fever or sudden illness needs urgent oncology advice. Do not wait for a scan, an online answer or the next clinic visit.

items.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
items.text: Tell the surgical, dental, anaesthetic or imaging team if you have a hormone-producing NET or a previous hormone crisis. Ask your specialist whether special preparation is needed. Carry your current medicines and emergency plan; the wallet card supports this information but does not replace specialist instructions.

before.title: Your overall plan and choices
before.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment plan.

items.title: What are we trying to achieve?
items.text: Ask whether the main aim is to slow growth, reduce tumour size, relieve hormone symptoms, make another treatment possible or protect day-to-day quality of life. The aim and likely benefit depend on your particular NET and previous treatment. A stable scan may represent useful control even without tumour shrinkage.

items.title: How treatments fit together
items.text: Some people need surgery, hormone-control treatment, tablets, chemotherapy, PRRT, liver-directed treatment or external radiotherapy at different points. These are not all automatically part of your regimen. Ask the multidisciplinary team to draw your own sequence and name the clinician coordinating it.

items.title: Choosing between options
items.text: Ask why this option suits your tumour site, grade, growth rate, symptoms, receptor status and other health conditions. Discuss alternatives, the option of observation when appropriate, supportive care, and any suitable clinical trial. A treatment listed in a US guide is not a guarantee of availability or funding in Ireland.

items.title: Evidence is about groups
items.text: A trial can measure time before cancer worsens, tumour shrinkage or survival. These are different outcomes. A group result does not predict your own response or lifespan. Ask how closely the study patients match your diagnosis and what benefit would make the treatment worthwhile to you.

items.title: Review points and shared decisions
items.text: Agree when you will review symptoms, tests and scans, and what would lead to continuing, delaying, changing or stopping treatment. Discuss work, caring duties, travel and the effects you most want to avoid. You can revisit your choices as your situation changes.

before.title: Eating, energy, practical help and support
before.intro: Supportive care can be used alongside treatment from the start.

items.title: Food, weight and digestion
items.text: Tell the team about weight loss, poor appetite, early fullness, persistent diarrhoea or greasy stools. Ask for a dietitian familiar with NETs and your surgery or medicines. Different causes need different support; do not assume every bowel symptom needs the same diet or medicine. Ask whether digestive-enzyme assessment or replacement is relevant to you.

items.title: Fluids and safe activity
items.text: Follow your individual fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea, kidney disease or heart problems. Balance manageable activity with rest. Tell the team if fatigue, dizziness, pain or breathlessness limits usual tasks; these symptoms can have treatable causes.

items.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
items.text: Living with repeated tests and treatment can affect sleep, mood, relationships and confidence. Ask about psychological support, sexual health, fertility advice, symptom-control services and support for carers. Supportive or palliative care aims to improve comfort and daily life and can accompany active anticancer treatment.

items.title: Practical help
items.text: Ask your nurse or social worker about transport, work, finances, home support, caring responsibilities and local NET support organisations. A general resource list may include services in other countries; your team can identify options available to you.

items.title: A record that works without a phone
items.text: Keep the printed schedule, medicine list, tests, contact numbers and written emergency instructions together. The full handbook contains the information in sequence for offline reading. The QR code is an optional route to more information; it is not needed to call for help or follow your paper plan.

items.title: Questions to take to the next visit
items.text: What is my exact diagnosis and grade? What is treatment trying to achieve? Which tests are mandatory for this medicine, and which depend on my NET? Who reviews results? What symptoms mean call now? What support would help me live as well as possible?

after.title: Later effects and continuing follow-up
after.intro: New or persistent symptoms still need review after the course.

items.title: Delayed effects
items.text: Kidney injury and rare bone-marrow disorders, including myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukaemia, can occur later. Persistent tiredness, infections, bruising or bleeding needs review even after the treatment course.

after.title: Hormone and fluid changes to watch for
after.intro: Use the urgent-contact instructions whenever symptoms occur.

items.title: Hormone crisis
items.text: PRRT can trigger a sudden hormone release. The treatment information highlights the first 48 hours as the main early-risk period. Staff monitor you and may give extra medicines or extend the stay. You need clear instructions for symptoms after discharge; a history of hormone symptoms affects planning.

items.title: Tumour breakdown and fluid changes
items.text: Rapid tumour breakdown can disturb blood chemistry. New muscle cramps, weakness, confusion, palpitations, reduced urine or breathlessness needs prompt assessment. Staff also monitor potassium and fluid balance around the amino-acid infusion.

after.title: Understanding your particular NET
after.intro: Several different features help the team choose treatment.

items.title: Where it started and where it is now
items.text: A neuroendocrine tumour begins in cells with hormone-making features. Its starting organ and the places it has spread are separate parts of the diagnosis. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour differs from pancreatic adenocarcinoma; a deposit in the liver may have come from another organ.

items.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
items.text: The pathology report describes how organised the cells look (differentiation) and their growth activity (grade). Ki-67 measures cells showing a growth-related protein in the sample. Its percentage describes that sample, not the amount of your body affected or your chance of survival.

items.title: Grade is different from stage
items.text: Stage describes extent; grade describes tumour biology. Either can vary independently. A well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumour and a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are distinct diagnoses and may need different treatments.

items.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
items.text: A functioning tumour produces a hormone syndrome. A nonfunctioning tumour can still cause problems through growth or pressure. Somatostatin receptor uptake on a scan shows a treatment target; it does not, on its own, identify a hormone syndrome.

items.title: Your diagnosis record
items.text: Ask for one diagnosis summary: starting organ, grade, differentiation, Ki-67 result if reported, sites involved, hormone syndrome and receptor-imaging result. Keep pending results clearly marked.

after.title: Making sense of tests and results
after.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and hormone tests answer different questions.

items.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
items.text: Blood counts assess oxygen-carrying cells, infection-fighting cells and platelets. Kidney and liver results help assess treatment safety. These checks are needed even when you feel well; a reassuring scan answers a different question.

items.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
items.text: CT and MRI show anatomy and tumour size. Somatostatin receptor imaging tests whether a particular receptor target is present. An FDG-PET scan measures uptake of a glucose-like tracer and is used selectively. Your team chooses the scans that can guide your care.

items.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
items.text: Selected markers may help answer a hormone or tumour question. Examples include 5-HIAA for serotonin-related symptoms, chromogranin A, or a specific pancreatic hormone. They are not a routine panel for every neuroendocrine tumour. Interpret changes with symptoms and imaging.

items.title: Preparing for a test
items.text: Use the laboratory instructions for fasting, food restrictions and any timed urine collection. Some medicines affect marker results, including acid-suppressing medicines and chromogranin A. Ask the team what to do; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself.

items.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
items.text: Some hormone syndromes can affect heart valves, so an ultrasound of the heart may be requested. Inherited-risk assessment depends on the tumour and family history; multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is one example. An inherited-risk test and a test of tumour tissue answer different questions.

items.title: Who does what, and when?
items.text: For each test, write its name, purpose, booking date and result-review contact. Ask the team to set your next scan or marker date. A schedule for someone after surgery may not apply during your treatment.

after.title: Hormone symptoms and day-to-day changes
after.intro: A new symptom may come from the NET, treatment or another illness.

items.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
items.text: Keep a brief record of your usual bowel pattern, flushing, appetite, weight, pain and energy. Note new changes and when they started. This helps the team assess whether treatment, hormones or another problem needs attention.

items.title: Hormone-related symptoms
items.text: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.

items.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
items.text: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.

items.title: When a change is urgent
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency plan for sudden or severe symptoms. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency assessment. Severe diarrhoea, persistent vomiting, dehydration, fever or sudden illness needs urgent oncology advice. Do not wait for a scan, an online answer or the next clinic visit.

items.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
items.text: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.

after.title: Your overall plan and choices
after.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment plan.

items.title: What are we trying to achieve?
items.text: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.

items.title: How treatments fit together
items.text: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.

items.title: Choosing between options
items.text: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.

items.title: Evidence is about groups
items.text: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.

items.title: Review points and shared decisions
items.text: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.

after.title: Eating, energy, practical help and support
after.intro: Supportive care can be used alongside treatment from the start.

items.title: Food, weight and digestion
items.text: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.

items.title: Fluids and safe activity
items.text: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.

items.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
items.text: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.

items.title: Practical help
items.text: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.

items.title: A record that works without a phone
items.text: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.

items.title: Questions to take to the next visit
items.text: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.

after.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
after.text: Lutathera can harm an unborn child and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for seven months after the last dose for patients who could become pregnant; men with partners who could become pregnant need contraception during treatment and for four months afterwards. Breastfeeding must stop before treatment; follow specialist advice.

after.title: If a visit is delayed
after.text: Low blood counts, kidney or liver changes, other side effects or a change in the cancer may lead the specialist to postpone, reduce or stop treatment. A four-stamp record shows planned administrations, not medical clearance. A dose does not automatically become suitable at the maximum interval. Keep the blood-test and symptom plan while waiting for the team’s decision.

after.title: Contacts and paperwork
after.text: Write the actual NET, PRRT nursing and radiation-protection contacts on the paper plan. Example numbers are not clinical contact lines. Keep the written precautions and urgent hormone-symptom instructions with the discharge letter.

after.title: Your specialist team’s scan appointments
after.text: Radiation-assessment scans measure where the treatment went and the radiation delivered to organs. They answer a different question from CT or MRI scans of tumour response. The detailed treatment information describes three radiation scans on separate days in the first week after the first infusion, starting the next day, and one after later infusions; response CT or MRI is described between the second and third infusions and after the course. Confirm your actual bookings with the team: these are service arrangements, not a universal timetable for every neuroendocrine tumour.

after.title: Extra blood tests after the course
after.text: Blood counts, kidney and liver tests continue every four weeks for at least three months after the last administration, then every three months for the following year. Your written discharge plan may also include two-weekly tests for the first eight weeks after the last infusion. The team confirms those extra early appointments and who reviews the results.

changes.before: This is the NCCP blood-test sequence with EMA potassium safety and the Irish PRRT service pathway. The post-infusion radiation-assessment scan is different from a response scan. The service confirms bookings, exact dates and any additional follow-up.
changes.after: This is the NCCP blood-test sequence with EMA potassium safety and the PRRT service pathway. The post-infusion radiation-assessment scan is different from a response scan. The service confirms bookings, exact dates and any additional follow-up.

after.label: Full blood count
after.timing: Before treatment; once 2–4 weeks before and shortly before each administration; every 2 weeks between treatments.
after.purpose: Checks haemoglobin, white cells with differential, and platelets.
after.detail: After the last administration: every 4 weeks for at least 3 months, then every 3 months for the following year. Your written plan may include extra early checks.
after.scope: routine

after.label: Kidney function
after.timing: With the blood-test schedule above; monitor for at least the first year after treatment.
after.purpose: Serum creatinine and calculated creatinine clearance assess kidney safety.
after.detail: The team calculates clearance using the required method. A normal symptom check does not replace these tests.
after.scope: routine

after.label: Liver function
after.timing: With the blood-test schedule above.
after.purpose: Tests include ALT, AST, albumin, bilirubin and INR to assess liver function and protein production.
after.scope: routine

after.label: Potassium
after.timing: Before the kidney-protective amino-acid infusion; further checks if indicated.
after.purpose: Detects potassium disturbances that the amino-acid infusion can worsen.
after.scope: routine

after.label: Heart pumping assessment
after.timing: Before starting, as specified in the regimen.
after.purpose: An echocardiogram or MUGA scan assesses heart pumping function.
after.scope: routine

after.label: 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
after.timing: Only if requested for your hormone syndrome; the team sets the dates.
after.purpose: Measures a breakdown product of serotonin to help assess selected neuroendocrine tumours.
after.detail: Often a timed urine collection. Follow the laboratory’s food and medicine instructions.
after.scope: conditional

after.label: Chromogranin A
after.timing: Only when the team considers it informative for your tumour.
after.purpose: A selected tumour-marker result, interpreted with symptoms and scans.
after.detail: Acid-suppressing medicines and other conditions can alter the result. It is not a routine test before every treatment; do not stop medicines yourself.
after.scope: conditional

after.label: Selected pancreatic hormones
after.timing: Only for the hormone question identified by your specialist.
after.purpose: Examples include gastrin, insulin or glucagon when the diagnosis or symptoms call for them.
after.detail: The team names the test, preparation and review date; these are not a standard panel for every patient.
after.scope: conditional

changes.before: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.
changes.after: Agree who can help with medicines, travel and appointments if memory, sight, fatigue or hand strength makes them difficult. Record your preferences and consent for sharing information.

changes.before: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.
changes.after: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.

changes.before: Lomustine and procarbazine have moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Vincristine alone has minimal emetic risk. The team supplies a day-specific anti-sickness plan, including the procarbazine days, and a rescue plan. Vincristine can slow the bowel through its effect on nerves. Preventive laxatives are recommended in NCCP; follow the prescribed plan and report constipation early. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind needs urgent advice. Procarbazine has important interactions. Avoid alcohol during treatment and follow the pharmacist’s written food restrictions and advice about when restrictions end. Check all prescription, over-the-counter, herbal and supplement products before taking them. Keep any prescribed seizure medicine and steroid plan separate from the PCV calendar. Report new weakness, tingling, gait change or constipation before vincristine. A medicine review is needed before adding any treatment for symptoms.
changes.after: Lomustine and procarbazine have moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Vincristine alone has minimal emetic risk. The team supplies a day-specific anti-sickness plan, including the procarbazine days, and a rescue plan. Vincristine can slow the bowel through its effect on nerves. Preventive laxatives are recommended in NCCP; follow the prescribed plan and report constipation early. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind needs urgent advice. Procarbazine has important interactions. Avoid alcohol during treatment and follow the pharmacist’s written food restrictions and advice about when restrictions end. Check all prescription, over-the-counter, herbal and supplement products before taking them. Keep prescribed steroids and seizure medicines on a separate plan from chemotherapy. Before vincristine, report new weakness, tingling, walking difficulty or constipation. Check new symptom medicines with the team.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-brain-patient

changes.before: Gliomas begin in supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different diagnoses. A tumour that spread to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and is not covered by these glioma regimens. Record the exact integrated diagnosis and where it is located.
changes.after: A glioma is a tumour arising in the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different types. Cancer that travels to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and follows a different pathway.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: nci-cns

changes.before: nci-cns
changes.after: ed-eano

changes.before: Grade describes features linked to how a tumour behaves. Adult gliomas are usually discussed by their type, grade and molecular findings rather than the stage system used for many other cancers. Grade 4 does not mean cancer has spread through the body. Ask your specialist to explain your own report and any older terminology in the treatment protocol.
changes.after: Glioma reports combine the tumour type, grade and molecular findings. Grade is not a measure of spread around the body: a grade 4 brain tumour does not mean body-wide metastases. Ask your specialist to explain older terms in your records.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-brain-molecular

changes.before: IDH1 or IDH2 changes and loss of parts of chromosomes 1p and 19q help classify particular gliomas. The combination of findings matters: one result should not be read in isolation. These tests are usually performed on tumour tissue. They do not automatically mean a change has been inherited or that relatives need testing.
changes.after: Changes in the IDH genes and loss of chromosome regions 1p and 19q help classify certain gliomas. The pattern of results matters. These are usually tumour-sample tests; they do not by themselves show that a change runs in the family.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-brain-molecular

changes.before: MGMT is involved in repairing certain DNA damage. Methylation of its promoter can reduce that repair activity and helps the team discuss the likely benefit of temozolomide in relevant settings. It is not a blood tumour marker, a percentage of tumour left, or an individual survival prediction. Record the reported result and ask how it affects your treatment choice.
changes.after: The MGMT gene makes a protein that repairs a particular type of DNA damage. Methylation in its control region can reduce that repair and inform discussion of temozolomide benefit. This is a tumour-tissue result, not a blood marker or a personal survival percentage.

changes.before: Keep the biopsy or operation date, pathology wording, grade, IDH result, 1p/19q result and MGMT result if tested. Mark a result as pending or not applicable rather than assuming it is negative. Ask whether specialist pathology review or further testing would change the plan.
changes.after: Keep the exact pathology diagnosis, sample date, grade and available molecular results together. Label a result as pending or not tested when appropriate. Ask whether further pathology review would affect the plan.

changes.before: A full blood count checks infection-fighting white cells, oxygen-carrying red cells and platelets that help stop bleeding. Kidney and liver tests help assess treatment safety. Attend the regimen’s required tests even when you feel well; a reassuring scan does not replace them. The schedule in this guide separates checks before, during and after treatment.
changes.after: A full blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests assess other aspects of treatment safety. Follow the blood-test schedule even when you feel well or the scan is reassuring.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-brain-patient

changes.before: MRI is the main scan used to assess many gliomas. Your team also considers symptoms, strength, movement, speech, memory, daily function and medicines such as steroids. Tell staff before MRI about implants or metal, kidney problems, previous contrast reactions or difficulty lying still. Ask about support if scans make you anxious.
changes.after: MRI gives detailed pictures of the brain. The team also checks symptoms, movement, speech, thinking and daily function. Before scanning, tell staff about implants, metal, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and ask for help if the scan worries you.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-rano

changes.before: After treatment, inflammation and other treatment effects can resemble tumour growth on MRI. This is sometimes called pseudoprogression. The team may need comparison scans, specialist imaging or further assessment before deciding what a change means. New or worsening symptoms still need prompt review; do not assume they are harmless treatment effects.
changes.after: Treatment-related changes can resemble tumour growth on MRI; this is called pseudoprogression. The specialist interprets the scan with symptoms and may need another scan or further assessment. Report worsening symptoms promptly rather than assuming a scan change is harmless.

changes.before: Write the next MRI date, what question it should answer and who will explain the result. Timing depends on your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous findings. General follow-up intervals in an international booklet are not automatically your schedule. These regimens do not require a generic CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or a blood tumour marker before every cycle.
changes.after: Record the next MRI and the contact who will explain it. Your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous results determine the interval. Other scans or blood markers are ordered for a specific reason, not automatically before every cycle.

changes.before: Use the passport to distinguish a test being booked, completed and reviewed. Record the agreed next step and whom to call if an appointment or result is missing. Do not alter chemotherapy or steroids yourself in response to a number or scan report.
changes.after: Mark tests as booked, done and reviewed so the next action is clear. Contact the named service about a missing result. Do not change chemotherapy or steroids in response to a report without instructions.

changes.before: Write down your usual headache, strength, walking, speech, vision, memory, mood, sleep and seizure pattern before treatment. Note new changes, when they started and how they affect daily tasks. With your permission, a trusted person can help spot changes or record what happened.
changes.after: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.

changes.before: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions.
changes.after: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: nhs-dexamethasone

changes.before: nhs-dexamethasone
changes.after: ed-eano

changes.before: Steroids may be prescribed to reduce swelling around the tumour. They are not automatically needed for everyone. Ask for the exact dose, time, review date and any taper plan. Do not stop or change them suddenly without advice. Report sleep or mood changes, increased thirst, infection symptoms or muscle weakness and ask which additional checks or protection you need.
changes.after: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-eano

changes.before: If prescribed, take seizure medicines on the agreed schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and whom to contact for breakthrough symptoms. Some medicines can affect mood, alertness or interact with treatment. Do not start, stop or switch them yourself. A rescue medicine needs an individual plan and training for whoever may give it.
changes.after: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.

changes.before: Ask your clinical team about driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery in light of your symptoms and any seizures. Local medical and licensing rules need individual advice; this guide does not give a universal driving clearance date. Occupational therapy can help adapt daily routines and the home.
changes.after: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.

changes.before: Surgery or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and follow-up have different jobs. Ask your team to draw the intended sequence and identify where you are now. Concurrent treatment means treatments overlap; adjuvant treatment follows the main treatment. A change of phase may change the dose, blood tests and support medicines.
changes.after: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.

changes.before: Ask whether the aim is to control the tumour, delay growth, relieve symptoms, preserve function or a combination of these. Discuss likely benefits, burdens, alternatives and what would prompt a pause or stop. The answer depends on the exact diagnosis, previous treatment and your priorities.
changes.after: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.

changes.before: Clinical trials describe groups of people and may use older pathology names or different schedules. They cannot predict one person’s response or lifespan. Ask how closely the evidence matches your tumour and treatment. No benefit number from one schedule should automatically be applied to another.
changes.after: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.

changes.before: Ask about appropriate clinical trials, specialist opinions, symptom support and other treatment options. A medicine or device described in an international guide is not automatically licensed, funded or suitable in Ireland. The treating multidisciplinary team explains what is available and relevant.
changes.after: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.

changes.before: Bring up fatigue, thinking, independence, family time, work, travel and side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for information at a pace and in a format that suits you. You may ask for a trusted person to join the discussion, written notes and time to reconsider decisions.
changes.after: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-brain-patient

changes.before: Tell the team about word-finding, attention, memory, reading, vision or planning difficulties. Rehabilitation may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, or neuropsychological support. Written routines, rest breaks and help with medicine organisation can make day-to-day care more manageable.
changes.after: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.

changes.before: Report poor appetite, weight change, vomiting or constipation early. Ask for dietitian help if eating is difficult. Use the prescribed anti-sickness and bowel plan; do not wait until symptoms are severe. Choose activity that is safe for your balance and strength and balance it with rest. Ask about treatable causes of fatigue.
changes.after: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.

changes.before: Anxiety, low mood, changes in behaviour and uncertainty can affect both patients and carers. Tell the team what has changed and ask for appropriate psychological or social support. Carers may need their own information, practical help and breaks. Agree who the team may share information with.
changes.after: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.

changes.before: Ask the specialist nurse or social worker about getting to treatment, time off work, benefits, caring responsibilities and support at home. Plan who can help with daily capsules and appointments if your memory, vision or fatigue makes these difficult.
changes.after: Plan travel, time away from work, caring duties and help with appointments. A nurse or social worker can identify practical support; agree who can help with tablets if needed.

changes.before: nccn-patient
changes.after: ed-palliative

changes.before: Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life while active treatment continues. You can discuss future care preferences and who you want involved in decisions at a time that suits you. Ask the team for Irish advice and documentation rather than using legal or hospice rules from a US booklet.
changes.after: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.

changes.before: Keep the printed schedule, current medicine list, tests, contact numbers and emergency instructions together. This handbook can be read in sequence without internet access. The wallet card and optional QR code help others find the regimen information; they do not replace your prescription or emergency plan.
changes.after: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.

changes.before: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.
changes.after: Agree who can help with medicines, travel and appointments if memory, sight, fatigue or hand strength makes them difficult. Record your preferences and consent for sharing information.
